2.content: Freeze the next state deeply with enableAutoFreeze, so that accidental changes to it fail.

7.content: Mutative leaves the next state unfrozen by default. With the `enableAutoFreeze` option, it freezes the next state deeply with `Object.freeze()`, so that code that changes the state by accident fails instead of changing a state that other code still uses.

8.content: Set it for a whole application with `makeCreator()`, and pass it to `apply()` to freeze the states that patches produce.

9.content: Every object of the next state that its enumerable keys reach: the copies of the objects that the recipe changed, the values that it assigned, and the objects that the next state shares with the base state, which are frozen in the base state as well. A recipe that changes nothing returns the base state itself, frozen.

10.content: Class instances, dates and functions, which `Object.freeze()` freezes like any object. A `Date` keeps its setters, such as `setFullYear()`, since its value is not a property.

11.content: Maps and Sets, whose `set()`, `add()`, `delete()` and `clear()` methods then throw, and the objects that a Map uses as keys.

12.content: Objects that are already frozen are skipped together with the values they hold, so after the first update freezes the state, each later update freezes only the objects that it copied or added. A base state may be frozen already: Mutative copies frozen objects when a recipe changes them, as it copies any other object.

13.content: Writing to a frozen object throws a `TypeError` in strict mode code, which includes ES modules and classes, and does nothing elsewhere. A frozen Map or Set throws in either case.

14.content: Development builds throw for a next state that holds a circular reference, an object that holds itself through its values, which Mutative does not support; see Shared references. Production builds skip this check.

15.content: With auto-freeze, production builds also skip frozen objects when they search a returned value for drafts, so returning an earlier, frozen state costs little. Development builds still search them and throw when they find a draft there.

16.content: Freezing visits every object that is not frozen yet, so it costs time on every update, most of all for states that change wide objects or large arrays. In the benchmark, Immer, which freezes by default, took longer with auto-freeze than without it in most of the selected workloads, and Mutative's defaults leave it off.

17.content: Enable auto-freeze in development to catch accidental changes to the state, and leave it off in production for speed: `makeCreator({ enableAutoFreeze: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' })`. Keep it on in production if other code relies on a frozen state.

18.content: A mark that returns a custom shallow copy function cannot be combined with auto-freeze. `current()` returns unfrozen snapshots, also with auto-freeze, and TypeScript types the result of `create()` with `enableAutoFreeze: true` as `Immutable<State>`, whose properties are `readonly`.

20.content: Create producers that take the base state and more arguments, and drafts that you finalize later.

23.content: Besides `create(base, recipe)`, `create()` has two curried forms: a recipe alone gives a producer, a function that takes the base state later, and a base state alone gives a draft that you finalize later.

24.content: `create(recipe, options?)` returns a producer, `(base, ...args) => nextState`. The producer drafts its first argument and passes the draft and its other arguments to the recipe:

25.content: A producer with an action argument is a reducer, for Redux, `useReducer()` or any other library that takes one:

26.content: The options of the call apply to every state that the producer makes, so `create(recipe, { enablePatches: true })` gives a producer that returns `[nextState, patches, inversePatches]`.

27.content: The producer calls the recipe with its own `this`, so it can be a method.

28.content: A producer of an async recipe returns a Promise of the next state.

29.content: In TypeScript, annotate the type of the draft parameter, as above, to type the producer's parameters and result.

30.content: `create(base, options?)` returns a draft of the base state and a `finalize()` function, for changes that do not fit in one recipe, such as changes spread over several functions. `finalize()` returns what `create()` returns with a recipe:

31.content: The base state must be draftable here, since no recipe returns a value instead.

32.content: Call `finalize()` only once. When it throws, for example because a development build rejects a patch path, the drafts are not revoked as they are when a recipe fails: they stay writable, and a second `finalize()` returns a state that can hold a revoked draft, with patches that miss changes. Create a new draft from the base state instead.

33.content: The `create()` function of `makeCreator()` has the same forms, with its default options.

35.content: Freezing, currying, marks, patches, strict mode, TypeScript, pitfalls, performance, and migration from Immer and from Mutative v1.

37.content: Decide with the mark option which values Mutative drafts, which it leaves mutable, and how it copies them.

42.content: By default, Mutative drafts plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets, and leaves every other value as it is: a class instance, a `Date` or an object without a prototype in the state is shared by the draft, the base state and the next state. The `mark` option changes that for the values you choose, without changing the values or their classes.

43.content: A mark is a function that receives each value that a recipe reads from a draft, and `{ mutable: 'mutable', immutable: 'immutable' }`. It returns:

44.content: `'immutable'` to draft the value, such as a class instance. Mutative copies it when the recipe changes it, keeping its prototype.

45.content: `'mutable'` to keep the value out of drafts. The recipe reads and changes the value itself, and every value that it holds, and the next state shares it.

46.content: A function that returns a shallow copy of the value, to draft it with that copy.

47.content: Nothing, to draft the value as usual.

48.content: Pass a list of marks to combine them: the first one that returns a value decides, as in `mark: [markSimpleObject, markTodos]`. `markSimpleObject()` is a mark for objects without a prototype and plain objects of other realms.

49.content: Use the same marks for every call on the same state: `makeCreator({ mark })` sets them as defaults, and `apply()` and `isDraftable()` take them as an option. A base state that is a class instance needs an `immutable` mark, or `create()` throws.

50.content: Values marked `immutable` work with patches and auto-freeze like plain objects, and so does a mark that makes every object immutable, as `() => 'immutable'` does.

51.content: A mark that returns a copy function cannot be combined with patches or auto-freeze, which development builds report with an error, and some patches might not apply to such values.

52.content: In strict mode, reading a value marked `mutable` from a draft throws outside `unsafe()`, as reading any value that is not drafted does.

53.content: A mark that returns a function drafts the value with the copy that the function returns, for values that the default copy does not handle, such as a `Date`:

54.content: The first read of such a value returns its copy itself, and later reads return a draft of the copy. Changes through either reach the next state, but the methods of a `Date`, and of other objects that keep their data in internal slots or private fields, work only on the copy itself, so read such a value once and change it through that reference, as the recipe above does. To change a `Date` without a mark, assign a new one instead.

55.content: Mutative copies an instance that `mark` makes `immutable` with all its own properties, non-enumerable ones included, and reads its own accessors as values, as Immer's `setUseStrictShallowCopy('class_only')` does. To copy quickly, it assigns the own properties that are enumerable, writable and configurable instead of defining them, as Immer's default copy does. An own property that shadows a setter of its class, such as a class field over an accessor of a base class, therefore runs that setter on the copy, which can change objects that the copy shares with the base state, and one that shadows a getter without a setter or a read-only property makes the copy throw. Keep such values in accessors of the class or under other keys.

56.content: Migration from Mutative v1 to v2

57.content: The changes since Mutative 1.3.0 that can affect existing code, in builds, patches, arrays, returned values, development builds, types and fixes.

65.content: Mutative v2 keeps the v1 API. The changes below, made since v1.3.0, can affect existing code.

66.content: **ES2018 output.** Every build targets ES2018 instead of ES2015, so object spread stays native. Engines that support Proxy but not ES2018 syntax, such as Chrome 49–59, Firefox 18–54, Safari 10–11.0 and Edge 12–18, need Mutative transpiled by your build.

67.content: **Bundlers.** The ESM entry compares `process.env.NODE_ENV` at each development check instead of always running development code. Production bundles, in which the bundler defines `NODE_ENV` as `production`, drop the development checks and warnings and throw minified errors, as CommonJS consumers already did. Bundles that target Node.js without defining `NODE_ENV`, such as esbuild with `platform: 'node'`, now include both CommonJS builds; define `NODE_ENV` or keep Mutative external.

68.content: **Node.js ESM.** In Node.js, `import` resolves a module that re-exports the CommonJS build, so `import` and `require` share one instance and both follow `NODE_ENV`. Previously, `import` always ran the development ESM build as a separate instance.

69.content: **Without a bundler.** `dist/mutative.esm.mjs` and `dist/mutative.esm.js` read `process.env.NODE_ENV` when they load, so loading them without a bundler, from a `<script type="module">` with a raw CDN URL or in another runtime without `process`, fails with `process is not defined`. Load `dist/mutative.esm.production.min.mjs` instead, or the UMD build that the `unpkg` and `jsdelivr` fields point to.

70.content: **Production errors.** Production builds throw `Minified Mutative error #<code>` with a link to the errors page instead of the full message, also for `apply()`, `original()` and `rawReturn()`. Development builds keep the messages. Code that matches error messages in production must match the codes instead.

71.content: **Order.** The patches of a nested draft now come before those of its parents, the order Immer uses. For example, `const item = draft.list[0]; draft.list.length = 0; item.text = 'b'; draft.item = item;` yields the `list` length replace before the `item` add. Applying the patches gives the same state as before, and replace patches that only restated an unchanged draft at its original index are no longer emitted.

72.content: **Values.** A patch value that was a draft is now the object that the next state holds instead of a deep copy, and it is frozen with the state when `enableAutoFreeze` is on. `apply()` still copies patch values before applying them. Copy a patch value before mutating it.

73.content: **Moved drafts.** A changed draft that leaves its key, because `sort()` or an assignment moved it or another value replaced it there, no longer emits patches under its old path; the patches of its parent carry its value. In v1, the patches of such a recipe could fail to apply, for example the inverse patches once a primitive took the old key.

74.content: **Set items.** A changed item of a Set that also added or removed items is carried by the Set's `remove` and `add` patches. v1 also emitted patches under the item's position in the changed Set, which replay applied to whatever sat at that position in the base Set, or could not apply at all. A Set that only changed its items keeps the patches under each item's position.

75.content: **Original objects assigned over drafts.** Assigning the original object of a draft to the key that holds the draft is recorded like any other assignment: when the draft was read at that key, the key holds its original value again and emits no patch; when the draft was moved there from another key, the key emits the patch of that assignment. In v1, both cases emitted a `remove` patch for an object key that the state kept, and the second emitted no patch for an array element, so replaying the patches dropped the key or lost the element.

76.content: `shift`, `unshift`, `splice` and `reverse` run natively on the draft's copy of a plain array, and `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf` and `includes` search it natively; see which array methods run natively. For data arrays, the results are those of v1 and the patches replay in both directions. An accessor property on an array index is read as a data value, so its getter may run a different number of times.

77.content: `current()` of a changed array copies the current array instead of reading every element through the draft. Base elements that a native method moved and that hold drafts of an outer `create()` call are left as they are, as unmoved elements always were.

78.content: To search a large array without drafting each element it visits, search `current(draft.list)` and change the match through the draft; see `current()`.

79.content: With `enableAutoFreeze`, production builds no longer search frozen objects in a value returned from a recipe, the returned value included, or the values they hold, for drafts, and leave a draft there unresolved. Development builds still search them and throw when they find one, also in an unfrozen object that a frozen one holds, where v1 replaced it. Never put a draft in a frozen object or in a value it holds. Without auto-freeze, returned values are searched as in v1.

80.content: In strict mode, development builds warn once when a recipe leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged, as a search through a large draft array does.

81.content: In strict mode, `rawReturn()` of a value without drafts no longer prints contradictory warnings.

82.content: Development builds warn once when `create()` receives a draft with a recipe, since it drafts a copy of the draft's current state, `current(draft)`, as v1 did; see `create()` on a draft.

83.content: With `enablePatches: { pathAsArray: false }`, development builds throw when a patch path would hold a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key, as a string path cannot name such a key: applying the patch writes another key, for example `'1'` instead of `1`, or fails for a change below that key. Production builds still generate such patches, as v1 did, and still throw a `TypeError` for a symbol key. Keep the default array paths for such keys.

84.content: With `enableAutoFreeze`, development builds report a circular reference only for an object that holds itself. A changed draft that holds its original, as `draft.prev = original(draft)` makes it, or that links to a shared object through another path no longer throws; production builds always froze such states. For a real cycle, the error names the path of the object that repeats, which can be one key longer than in v1.

85.content: Development builds throw when a recipe passes a draft to the `set()` method of a Map draft, as in `draft.map.set(draft.key, value)`: Map keys are used as they are, so the next state would keep the draft as a key, revoked, and reading its properties would throw. Production builds still keep such a key, as v1 did. Use `original(draft)`, `current(draft)` or an id as the key.

86.content: `create()` with an explicit state type and an async recipe, such as `create<State>(base, async (draft) => { … })`, returns `Promise<State>`, and so do curried producers; v1 typed the result as `State`. A state type that is a type parameter, as in a generic function, or that includes Promises, such as `object` or `unknown`, still gives the state type for async recipes and for recipes that may return a Promise, as in v1; leave out the type argument in generic code.

87.content: `apply()` accepts `enableAutoFreeze: true` and then returns `Immutable<State>`, as `apply<State, true>()` does; v1 rejected the option and typed the frozen result as mutable. With `enableAutoFreeze` typed as `boolean` or optional `true`, the result is `State | Immutable<State>`. With `mutable` typed as `boolean`, optional `boolean`, or optional `true`, `apply()` returns `State | void`.

88.content: A curried producer whose recipe annotates its draft and returns a new state, such as `create((draft: State) => ({ ...draft, count: 0 }))`, returns `State`, or `Promise<State>` for an async recipe. v1 typed such a call as a manual draft, so calling the producer did not compile. A recipe whose draft is annotated with a type parameter, as in `create((draft: T) => { … })` in a generic function, also gives a producer, which v1 typed as a manual draft as well.

89.content: With an explicit state type, a recipe that may or may not return a Promise, such as one typed `(draft: State) => void | Promise<void>`, gives `State | Promise<State>`, also for a primitive state type, such as `number`, and in curried producers and creators from `makeCreator()`. v1 typed the result as `State`.

90.content: With `enablePatches`, every changed item of a Set keeps its changes. In v1, when two or more items of a Set that was not the root changed below their first level, the state kept the change of only one of them.

91.content: A Set that receives an unchanged draft holds the original object, as the rest of the state does, instead of the draft's shallow copy.

92.content: A Set draft that the recipe moves to another place, such as another key, an array, a Map, another Set or a new object, keeps its added, deleted and changed items there when its old place gets another value or is removed; v1 kept its original items.

93.content: A draft of a Set subclass changes its copy, an instance of the subclass, as Map drafts do: the subclass's own `add`, `has`, `delete` and `clear` take effect during the recipe, while the draft iterates the items in the order in which the Set holds them. v1 kept the items of a changed Set in a separate map, which bypassed those methods until it rebuilt the Set after the recipe. As a Map subclass's `set` already had to in v1, a Set subclass's `add` must store the value that it receives: an `add` that stores a copy of a draft, or of an object that holds drafts, leaves those drafts in the next state, where reading them throws.

94.content: Assigning `undefined` to a key that `delete`, `shift`, `unshift` or a shrinking `splice` removed from a draft adds the key back; v1 left a hole or kept the shorter length.

95.content: Deleting an array index that the current draft does not own changes nothing, as in JavaScript. In v1, deleting an index already absent from the original array could create an `undefined` element and, if it was past the end, lengthen the array. This also fixes the v2.0.0 regression where deleting an index removed earlier in the same recipe grew the array again; v1 kept the shortened array (#212).

96.content: Assigning to a key that a draft holds as an own data property sets that property, as in JavaScript, also when a prototype defines a setter of that name. v1 called the setter through the draft instead, and assigning an own `__proto__` key, as `JSON.parse()` creates one, threw. A class instance that `mark` makes `immutable` is copied by assigning its own properties, so such a setter now runs on that copy instead of through the draft; see Copying marked instances.

97.content: Under a `mark` that returns `mutable`, a value that the recipe assigned or moved is read back as assigned, through the draft and in `current()`; v1 returned the original value.

98.content: `current()` of a draft whose state holds a plain Set with drafts returns a snapshot; v1 threw.

99.content: `current()` snapshots an object that the recipe assigned and that `mark` makes draftable, such as a class instance, together with the drafts it holds; v1 returned the object as it was, so a later change to those drafts showed through the snapshot.

100.content: With `enableAutoFreeze`, Map and Set instances are frozen too, so adding a property or replacing a method fails as on any frozen object; v1 only replaced their mutators. Later producers skip a frozen Map or Set instead of walking its entries again, and a Map or Set that holds itself no longer overflows the stack in production builds.

101.content: The iterators that Map and Set drafts return behave like built-in iterators: iterating one that was partly consumed continues where it stopped, and iterator helpers such as `toArray()` are available where the engine has them. In v1, iterating such an iterator started over, and only a Map's `keys()` had the helpers.

102.content: Consume Map value and entry iterators, and all Set iterators, while their draft is active. After the producer finishes or fails, or a manual draft is finalized, an iterator cannot yield another value and throws a `TypeError`. Lazy iterator helpers follow the same lifetime; an exhausted iterator stays exhausted. Map keys are not drafted, and `keys()` continues to return a native iterator.

103.content: `apply()` copies the own symbol keys of patch values, and an own `__proto__` key, as `JSON.parse()` creates one, stays a data property. v1 dropped symbol keys there and turned an own `__proto__` key into the prototype of the copy.

104.content: `apply()` rejects a patch whose path ends in `__proto__` on an object or array, as it rejects `__proto__` earlier in a path. Coercible property keys, such as a boxed string, are checked after conversion too. With `mutable: true`, v1 assigned the value and so replaced the prototype of the object.

105.content: In a patch path, `apply()` reads an item of a Set only at its index, such as `1` or `'1'`, and throws for any other key, such as `__proto__`. v1 read any property of an array of the Set's items there, which let a path through `__proto__` reach `Array.prototype`.

106.content: `apply()` with `mutable: true` throws for a patch that replaces the root state with another value, such as the patch of a recipe that returns a new state, as the state cannot be replaced in place. v1 ignored the replacement and applied the patches after it to the replacing value, so the state stayed as it was and the value of that patch changed.

107.content: An object that `mark` makes draftable, such as a plain object under `markSimpleObject`, keeps an own `__proto__` key, as `JSON.parse()` creates one, as a property of its copy; v1 assigned it, which replaced the prototype of the copy.

108.content: A patch for a Map key that is an array holds the key as one path segment; v1 spread the array into the path, so applying the patch wrote to other keys.

109.content: `apply()` uses a Map key of a patch path as it is. v1 converted it to a string first, which threw for an object without a prototype.

110.content: Array patches record a change between `0` and `-0`, which the state already kept; in v1, applying the patches lost the sign. An element that stays `NaN` no longer yields a replace patch.

111.content: Patches keep the holes of sparse arrays apart from `undefined` elements, in both directions. When a recipe shortens an array and lengthens it again, as `draft.length = 1; draft.length = 3` does, the patches shorten and lengthen the array as well, which leaves holes at the indices that the longer length exposes again, and the inverse patches put the removed elements back. In v1, applying the patches kept the removed elements at those indices, and applying the inverse patches left holes there. v1 also put `undefined` into the holes that an array got past its end, and where a recipe filled a hole, applying the inverse patches put `undefined` there.

112.content: In strict mode, a nested `unsafe()` call no longer ends the access of the outer call; in v1, reading mutable data after it in the outer callback threw.

113.content: A producer that fails after its recipe returned, for example because the recipe changed the draft and returned another value, revokes its drafts and releases its array method cache, as a recipe that throws does; v1 left them usable. This also covers errors while inspecting a returned Proxy or calling a returned Promise's `then` method, and preserves the original error.

114.content: A draft of an array whose `Symbol.isConcatSpreadable` is false copies its elements; v1 put the whole array into the copy as its only element.

116.content: Replace Immer's APIs with their Mutative counterparts, and check the defaults that differ.

125.content: Most code moves from Immer to Mutative by renaming functions: in both libraries a recipe changes a draft, and the next state shares every part that the recipe left unchanged. Comparison with Immer maps every Immer API to Mutative and lists the behaviors that differ.

126.content: mutative-compat wraps Mutative in Immer's API, for a quick switch before you migrate the calls themselves.

127.content: Replace `produce()` with `create()`, `produceWithPatches()` with `create()` and `enablePatches: true`, `applyPatches()` with `apply()`, and `nothing` with `rawReturn(undefined)`. `current()`, `original()`, `isDraft()`, `isDraftable()`, `castDraft()` and `castImmutable()` keep their names.

128.content: Remove the `enableMapSet()`, `enablePatches()` and `enableArrayMethods()` calls: Mutative supports Maps, Sets and patches without them, and runs array methods natively.

129.content: Decide about freezing. Immer freezes the next state by default, and Mutative does not. Code that relies on frozen state, for example to catch accidental mutations, needs `enableAutoFreeze: true`.

130.content: Replace the global configuration of `setAutoFreeze()` and `new Immer()` with options per call, or with defaults that `makeCreator()` sets.

131.content: Replace `[immerable] = true` on classes with the `mark` option.

133.content: Mutative leaves the next state unfrozen unless `enableAutoFreeze` is set, which also makes it faster. To keep Immer's default, pass the option to each call, or create a `create()` that has it:

134.content: A curried producer works the same way in both libraries: `produce(recipe)` becomes `create(recipe)`, and the producer passes its other arguments to the recipe; see Currying.

136.content: A patch listener passed to `produce()` becomes the same option: read the patches from the result of `create()`. The patches of both libraries differ for arrays that get shorter, which Mutative records as a `replace` of the `length` by default, and for objects changed in a Set; `enablePatches: { arrayLengthAssignment: false }` makes Mutative remove each index, as Immer does. See Patches in the comparison.

139.content: `createDraft()` and `finishDraft()` become one call of `create()` without a recipe, which returns the draft and the function that finalizes it:

141.content: Immer drafts the instances of a class that sets `[immerable] = true`. Mutative leaves classes unchanged and drafts the instances that a `mark` function makes `immutable`:

142.content: Pass the same `mark` to every `create()` and `apply()` call on such state, for example with `makeCreator({ mark })`. See Marking data structure.

143.content: Immer 11 does not support async recipes: one that changes the draft before its first `await` throws, because the returned Promise counts as a new value, and one that changes it later writes to a revoked draft. With Mutative, `create()` returns a Promise of the next state, and the draft stays usable until it settles:

144.content: `Draft<T>`, `Immutable<T>` and `Patch` are exported by both libraries, and Mutative adds `Patches`, the type of a list of patches, and `castMutable()`. Mutative infers the result type of `create()` from its options, such as the tuple of patches with `enablePatches: true`; see TypeScript.

146.content: Record the changes of a recipe as patches, and apply them to a state with apply().

155.content: With the `enablePatches` option, `create()` also returns the patches that turn the base state into the next state, and the inverse patches that turn the next state back into the base state. `apply()` applies them, for example to replay changes on another copy of the state, to send them over a network, or to undo and redo changes.

156.content: `enablePatches` also works with curried producers, manual drafts and `makeCreator()`, and it supports objects, arrays, Maps, Sets, and the values that a `mark` makes draftable; pass the same `mark` to `apply()`.

157.content: **Operations and paths.** Patches use `add`, `remove` and `replace`. A path leads from the root to the changed value through object keys, array indices, Map keys as they are, objects and arrays included, and the positions of Set items. A recipe that returns a new state gets one `replace` patch with an empty path.

158.content: **Order.** The patches of a nested draft come before those of its parents, as in Immer.

159.content: **Values.** A patch value is the object that the next state holds, frozen with it when `enableAutoFreeze` is on, so copy a patch value before changing it. `apply()` copies patch values before applying them.

160.content: **Arrays.** `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()`, `reverse()` and `sort()` emit a `replace` patch for each index whose element changed, and an `add` patch for each index past the old length. An array that gets shorter gets one `replace` patch of its `length` by default, or a `remove` patch for each index it loses with `arrayLengthAssignment: false`. Patches preserve holes in both directions: filling a hole takes a `replace` patch, and recreating one rebuilds the array from its index; see Sparse arrays.

161.content: **Maps.** `set()` emits an `add` patch for a new key and a `replace` patch for an existing one, and `delete()` a `remove` patch.

162.content: **Sets.** Patches add an item by its value and remove one by the value it holds; see Sets of objects.

163.content: **Moved drafts.** A changed draft that leaves its key, because `sort()` or an assignment moved it or another value replaced it there, emits no patches under its old path; the patches of its parent carry its value.

164.content: **Applying patches.** `apply()` applies `add`, `remove` and `replace` patches and accepts `-` as the index that appends to an array. It throws for other operations and for paths through `__proto__` or `constructor`. It takes the `enableAutoFreeze`, `strict` and `mark` options, or `mutable: true` to change the state in place, which throws for a patch that replaces the root state with another value, and it changes a draft in place.

165.content: **JSON Patch.** With `pathAsArray: false` and `arrayLengthAssignment: false`, patches of JSON-compatible objects and arrays are JSON Patch operations. Maps, Sets and array holes have no JSON counterpart.

166.content: Comparison with Immer lists where these patches differ from Immer's.

167.content: `enablePatches` takes `true`, or an object with two options that set the shape of the patches. With both set to `false`, patches of JSON-compatible objects and arrays are JSON Patch operations, which other JSON Patch libraries can apply (related discussion).

168.content: With `pathAsArray: false`, a path is a JSON Pointer string instead of an array of keys:

169.content: A string path holds only strings, so it cannot name a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key: with `pathAsArray: false`, the patch of `draft.set(1, 'b')` would set the key `'1'`. Keep the default array paths for such keys; development builds throw an error when a string path would hold one.

170.content: With `arrayLengthAssignment: false`, an array that gets shorter gets a `remove` patch for each index that it loses, instead of a `replace` patch of its `length`:

171.content: A `remove` patch per index takes more time and more patches for large arrays than one `replace` patch of the `length`, so leave `arrayLengthAssignment` on unless the patches must be JSON Patch operations.

172.content: A hole is an absent index, which differs from an own index whose value is `undefined`: array methods such as `map()` and `forEach()` skip holes. Patches and inverse patches preserve this distinction, including when a recipe lengthens an array, fills a hole with `undefined`, or moves holes with an array method.

173.content: An index patch carries a value, so it cannot represent a hole. Filling a hole takes a `replace` patch, but the patches that recreate a hole shorten the array to its index, lengthen it again to leave holes, and restore the elements after it, so their number grows with those elements: filling a hole before 10,000 elements yields one patch and 10,002 inverse patches. A recipe that makes a hole before the last element gets such patches, and inverse patches that fill it. Holes that an array gets past its old length need only a `replace` patch of its `length`. These patches preserve the array itself for mutable application and application on a draft, also inside a Set.

174.content: With `arrayLengthAssignment: false`, truncation still uses per-index `remove` patches, but recreating holes needs a `replace` patch of `length`. Apply these patches with Mutative's `apply()`: sparse arrays are JavaScript data, not JSON data, so their patches are not portable JSON Patch operations. JSON serialization turns array holes into `null` and cannot preserve their structure.

175.content: The inverse patches of each change undo it, and its patches redo it:

176.content: travels builds undo and redo with history limits, archives and persistence on these patches, and use-travel and zustand-travel bring it to React and Zustand.

177.content: Patches add a Set element by its value and remove one by the value it holds, so a `remove` patch removes an object only from a Set that holds that same object. A Set whose elements changed in place, without any element added or removed, gets patches under the position of each changed element, and they replay in both directions. Once a recipe adds or removes elements of a Set, the Set's `remove` and `add` patches carry every changed element by value instead. `apply()` copies the value of each patch before applying it, so a Set that `apply()` changes holds copies of the objects that patches add, and the inverse patches cannot remove those copies: an undo after a redo leaves the object in the Set. `apply()` also appends every element that it adds, so a Set that it changes can hold its elements in another order than the state that the recipe produced: a changed element of a Set that also added or removed elements, or an element that inverse patches add back, moves to the end, and a recipe that deletes an element and adds it back moves it to the end without a patch. The positions in the patches of a later recipe then find other elements, and its changes under them apply to another element without an error. Sets of primitives keep their elements, but their order can change in the same way. When patches are replayed on states that `apply()` returned, as undo, redo and synchronized copies do, keep such objects in a Map keyed by an id or in an array instead.

179.content: Write recipes that avoid needless drafts, searches, copies, freezing and patches.

180.content: Search large arrays in a snapshot

183.content: Make one update for related changes

185.content: Keep large data out of drafts

186.content: Mutative copies each object at most once per update and drafts only what a recipe reads, so most recipes are fast as they are. These tips help with large states and hot paths. The figures come from the benchmark on Node.js 24, in microseconds per update.

187.content: Every object that a recipe reads through a draft becomes a draft, so `draft.list.find()` creates a draft for each element it visits. Search `current(draft.list)`, which holds plain values, and change the match through the draft:

188.content: Updating the first of 10,000 rows and then finding and updating the last one took 176 µs this way and 2,169 µs through the draft. Take one snapshot for a series of searches: each call of `current()` copies the changed parts of the draft again. To read the base state without drafts, use `original()`.

189.content: Mutative searches a value that a recipe returns for drafts, which visits every object of it: returning a new state of 10,000 rows took 2,600 µs. When the value holds no drafts, such as a state built from scratch, wrap it in `rawReturn()`, which took 0.26 µs. Returning an earlier state is the one workload in which Immer's defaults were faster than Mutative's, since Immer freezes its states and skips frozen values in a returned state; see Performance compared with Immer.

190.content: `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()` and `reverse()` run natively on the copy of a plain array, while a loop that moves elements one by one goes through the draft for each of them. Removing the first of 10,000 rows with `shift()` took 7.04 µs, against 7,408 µs for Immer, which moves each element through its draft. See which array methods run natively.

191.content: Each `create()` call copies the objects on the path from the root to its changes, so several changes in one recipe copy shared parents once, where one call per change copies them each time. Group the changes of an action or an event into one recipe.

192.content: **Auto-freeze** visits every object of the next state that is not frozen yet. Inserting a property into an object of 1,000 properties took 50.3 µs without it and 140 µs with it. Enable it in development, or where other code relies on frozen state; see Auto Freeze.

193.content: **Patches** cost little when an update changes a few paths: pushing a row and inserting a property at 10,000 rows took 63.8 µs without them and 63.2 µs with them. Moving elements emits a patch for each moved index, so removing the first of 10,000 rows took 1,063 µs with patches. Keep `arrayLengthAssignment` on unless the patches must be JSON Patch operations, since a `remove` patch per index costs more than one `replace` of the `length`.

194.content: **Strict mode** inspects every value that a recipe reads, and sends array methods and `current()` through the draft for arrays that may hold objects. Enable it in development only; see Strict Mode.

195.content: Data that recipes read but never change, such as a large lookup table in the state, is drafted object by object as recipes read it. Read it with `original()`, or keep it outside the state. A mark that returns `'mutable'` for it keeps it out of drafts altogether, but then a recipe that changes it changes it in place.

207.content: Most recipes are ordinary JavaScript, but drafts are proxies that live only during their recipe, and Mutative copies only the values that it drafts. These are the mistakes that follow from that most often.

208.content: Assigning to the `draft` parameter only changes a local variable. To replace the whole state, return the new state:

209.content: A recipe either changes its draft or returns a new state. Doing both throws, because Mutative cannot tell which one is the next state; returning `undefined` or the draft itself keeps the changes. To make `undefined` the next state, return `rawReturn(undefined)`. Watch out for arrow functions that return the value of an assignment or of a method:

210.content: Mutative revokes the drafts of a recipe when it ends, so a draft that a callback, a closure or another state keeps throws when it is read later. Keep `current(draft)`, the original object, or the next state instead. The draft of an async recipe lives until its Promise settles, and that of `create(base)` until `finalize()` returns.

211.content: A draft also belongs to its own `create()` call: do not store it in the draft of another call; see create() on a draft.

212.content: Mutative drafts plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets. Other objects, such as class instances, dates and objects without a prototype, are shared by the draft, the base state and the next state, so a recipe that changes them changes the base state too:

213.content: Mark such classes as `immutable` so that Mutative drafts and copies their instances, use `markSimpleObject()` for objects without a prototype, or replace such values instead of changing them. Strict mode reports every read of such a value in development.

214.content: An object of the base state becomes a draft when the recipe reads it, so searching a draft array for the original object finds nothing. Search for an id, or search `original(draft)`, whose indices match the draft until the recipe adds, removes or moves elements:

216.content: When several paths of the state lead to the same object, each path gets a draft of its own, and the next state holds a copy for each path that changed. Assign one draft to the other paths to keep them shared; see Shared references.

217.content: `rawReturn()` returns a value without searching it for drafts, so a draft in it stays in the next state, revoked. Wrap only values without drafts, such as `rawReturn(initialState)`, and enable strict mode in development, which reports such drafts.

218.content: A patch value is an object that the next state holds, frozen with it when auto-freeze is on. Copy a patch value before changing it, or apply the patches with `apply()`, which copies patch values before applying them.

219.content: With auto-freeze, Mutative freezes the objects that the next state shares with the base state, so code that changes the base state in place afterwards fails, also for parts of it that the recipe did not change.

221.content: Make reads of values that Mutative does not draft explicit, and check returned values in development.

224.content: Mutative drafts plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets, and the values that a mark makes immutable. Every other object in the state, such as a `Date` or a class instance, is shared by the draft, the base state and the next state, so a recipe that changes it changes the base state as well. With the `strict` option, such reads become explicit.

Every object read through a draft becomes a draft, so a search through a large draft array, such as `draft.list.find()`, creates one for each element it visits. Search `current(draft.list)` instead and change the match through the draft.

239.content: `create()` infers the type of the state from the base state. The draft has the type `Draft<State>`, which removes `readonly` deeply, so a recipe can change state that is typed as readonly, and the result has the type of the base state:

242.content: With an explicit state type, TypeScript infers no other type argument, so pass `boolean` as the type argument for `enablePatches` when the options set it with a variable, as in `create<State, false, boolean>(base, recipe, options)`.

249.content: `castDraft(value)` types a value as a draft, for example to assign a readonly value into a draft.

250.content: `castImmutable(value)` types a value as `Immutable<T>`, for example an initial state that should be read only. It does not freeze the value.

251.content: `castMutable<T>(draft)` types a draft as `T`, for a function that requires `T` where `Draft<T>` does not fit, such as a class with private members, which a draft type lacks.

270.content: Apply patches to a state and get the next state, or change the state in place.

276.content: `apply()` applies patches, such as those that `create()` returns with `enablePatches`, and returns the next state. Like `create()`, it leaves the state as it was and shares every part that the patches do not change.

292.content: `enableAutoFreeze`, `strict` and `mark` work as the options of `create()` do. Pass `apply()` the same `mark` as the `create()` calls that generated the patches, so that it drafts the same values, such as class instances.

293.content: `mutable: true`, available since Mutative 1.2.0, changes the state in place instead, and `apply()` then returns `undefined`. It cannot be combined with the other options, which development builds report with a warning, and it throws for a patch that replaces the root state with another value, such as the patch of a recipe that returns a new state, because the state cannot be replaced in place.

294.content: Inside a recipe, `apply(draft, patches)` changes the draft in place and returns it, so patches can be combined with other changes in one update. It takes no options there.

295.content: `add`, `remove` and `replace` operations. Other operations, such as JSON Patch's `move`, `copy` and `test`, throw an error.

296.content: Paths as arrays of keys, or as JSON Pointer strings, such as those of `pathAsArray: false`. The index `-` appends to an array.

297.content: Map keys as they are, and Set items by value: `add` and `remove` patches add and remove the value that they hold, and a `replace` patch of a Set item throws. See Sets of objects.

298.content: A path through the `__proto__` or `constructor` of an object or array, or through the `prototype` of a function, throws, so that patches cannot change the prototypes of objects; Map keys of these names are ordinary keys. `apply()` reads the other path segments as properties, as Immer does, and does not guard against prototypes that other code has already changed.

299.content: A path that does not resolve throws an error that names it.

300.content: `apply()` copies the value of each patch deeply before applying it, so the next state does not share objects with the patches, and applying the same patches again gives another copy.

301.content: With `enableAutoFreeze: true`, `apply()` returns `Immutable<State>`, as `apply<State, true>()` does. With `enableAutoFreeze` typed as `boolean` or optional `true`, the result is `State | Immutable<State>`. With `mutable: true`, the result is `void`, and with `mutable` typed as `boolean`, optional `boolean`, or optional `true`, it is `State | void`.

302.content: The errors that `apply()` throws are listed with their production codes on the errors page.

304.content: castDraft(), castImmutable() and castMutable() change the TypeScript type of a value, and return the value as it is.

308.content: `castDraft()`, `castImmutable()` and `castMutable()` are helpers for TypeScript. Each returns its argument as it is, with another type, so they cost nothing at runtime and change nothing.

309.content: `castDraft(value)` types a value as a draft, `Draft<T>`, whose properties are not `readonly`. Use it to assign a value with readonly types into a draft:

310.content: The value is not drafted: the next state holds it as it is.

311.content: `castImmutable(value)` types a value as `Immutable<T>`, deeply readonly, for example an initial state that code should only read. It does not freeze the value; use auto-freeze for that.

312.content: `castMutable<T>(draft)` types a draft as `T`, for a function that requires `T` where `Draft<T>` does not fit. A draft type lacks the private members of a class, for example, so a draft of a class instance needs the cast where the class itself is expected:

313.content: TypeScript cannot infer `T` back from a `Draft<T>`, so pass it as a type argument, as above.

315.content: Produce the next state from the changes that a recipe makes to a draft of the base state.

327.content: `create()` drafts a base state, runs a recipe that changes the draft, and returns the next state. The next state shares every part that the recipe left unchanged with the base state, and the base state itself does not change.

328.content: `base` is the state to draft: a plain object, an array, a `Map`, a `Set`, or a value that the `mark` option makes draftable, such as a class instance. Other objects, such as dates and class instances that no mark makes draftable, throw an error. With a recipe, a primitive or `null` base is passed to the recipe as it is, and the value that the recipe returns is the next state.

329.content: `recipe` receives the draft, and in a producer also the other arguments of the producer. It changes the draft and returns nothing, or returns a new state. It can be an async function.

330.content: `options` are described below; `makeCreator()` sets their defaults.

331.content: `create()` returns the next state, which is the base state itself when the recipe changes nothing. With `enablePatches`, it returns `[nextState, patches, inversePatches]`: the patches turn the base state into the next state, and the inverse patches turn it back. For an async recipe, it returns a Promise of either.

345.content: `Mark \| Mark[]`, where `Mark` is `(target, { mutable, immutable }) => 'mutable' \| 'immutable' \| (() => copy) \| undefined`

347.content: In strict mode, reading an object that cannot be drafted from a draft, such as a `Date` or a class instance that no mark makes draftable, or a value that `mark` makes mutable, throws unless the read happens inside `unsafe()`. A value that the recipe returns with `rawReturn()` is still searched for drafts, and development builds warn when it holds one. In development builds, strict mode also warns once when a recipe leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged, as a search through a large draft array does; see `current()` for searching without creating drafts.

348.content: Strict mode checks every value that the recipe reads, so enable it in development and disable it in production, for example with `strict: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`.

349.content: `true` makes `create()` return `[nextState, patches, inversePatches]`; see Patches. An object sets the shape of the patches as well:

350.content: `pathAsArray`, `true` by default: a path is an array of keys, such as `['list', 0]`. With `false`, it is a JSON Pointer string, such as `'/list/0'`. A string path holds only strings, so it cannot name a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key: with `pathAsArray: false`, the patch of `draft.set(1, 'b')` would set the key `'1'`. Keep the default array paths for such keys; development builds throw an error when a string path would hold one.

351.content: `arrayLengthAssignment`, `true` by default: an array that gets shorter gets a `replace` patch of its `length`. With `false`, it gets a `remove` patch for each index that it loses, which takes more time for large arrays.

352.content: With `pathAsArray: false` and `arrayLengthAssignment: false`, the patches of objects and arrays are JSON Patch operations (RFC 6902); see the related discussion.

353.content: TypeScript types the result from the type of `enablePatches` in the options passed to `create()` or `makeCreator()`: `true` or an object gives `[state, patches, inversePatches]`, and `boolean` gives either. Options typed `{ enablePatches: true }` that may be `undefined`, such as an optional parameter of a wrapper, or typed `{ enablePatches?: true }` still give the tuple, although `create()` returns the state alone when patches are off; type the flag as `boolean` there. With an explicit state type, TypeScript infers no other type argument, so pass `boolean` as the type argument for `enablePatches` as well, as in `create<State, false, boolean>(base, recipe, options)` or `create<State, [], false, boolean>(recipe, options)`.

354.content: Freeze the next state deeply, also the parts that it shares with the base state, and, in development builds, throw for an object that holds itself; see Auto Freeze.

355.content: A mark decides how a value is drafted; see Marking data structure. It receives each value that the recipe reads and `{ mutable: 'mutable', immutable: 'immutable' }`, and returns:

356.content: `'immutable'` to make the value draftable, such as a class instance, which is then copied when the recipe changes it.

357.content: `'mutable'` to keep the value out of drafts: the recipe reads and changes it in place, as it does all the values that it holds.

358.content: A function that returns a shallow copy of the value, which drafts it with that copy. Patches and auto-freeze must be off, and some patches might not apply to such values.

359.content: `undefined` to draft the value as usual.

360.content: With an array of marks, the first one that returns a value decides. When a mark makes every object immutable, as `() => 'immutable'` does, patches and auto-freeze work as usual. An instance that `mark` makes `immutable` is copied with all its own properties, and those that are enumerable, writable and configurable are assigned, so an own property that shadows a setter of its class runs it, and one that shadows a getter or a read-only property throws; see Copying marked instances.

361.content: A recipe can return the next state instead of changing the draft:

362.content: Returning `undefined` or the draft itself keeps the changes made to the draft. To make `undefined` the next state, return `rawReturn(undefined)`.

363.content: A recipe that changes the draft and also returns another value throws an error.

364.content: Returning an unchanged child draft, such as `draft.list`, makes its value the next state; returning a changed one throws an error.

365.content: Mutative searches a returned object for drafts and replaces each one with its value, so a returned value can hold drafts, such as `{ ...draft, count: 0 }`. `rawReturn()` skips that search for a value that holds no drafts, and development builds warn when a returned object holds no drafts to suggest it.

366.content: The recipe can be an async function: `create()` then returns a Promise of the result, and the draft stays usable until that Promise settles.

367.content: `create()` recognizes the Promises of the current JavaScript realm only, so an async function from another realm, such as a `vm` context or an iframe, needs a wrapper from this realm: `create(baseState, async (draft) => { return await recipe(draft); })`. TypeScript types the result as a Promise as well, except with an explicit state type that is a type parameter, as in `create<T>(base, async (draft) => { … })` in a generic function, or that includes Promises, such as `object` or `unknown`, which gives the state type itself. In generic code, leave out the type argument: `create(base, async (draft) => { … })` gives `Promise<T>`, and `create(async (draft: T) => { … })` gives `(base: T) => Promise<T>`.

368.content: With a recipe and no base state, `create()` returns a producer, which takes the base state and passes its other arguments to the recipe:

369.content: With a base state and no recipe, `create()` returns a draft and a `finalize()` function, which returns what `create()` returns with a recipe:

370.content: Call `finalize()` only once. When it throws, for example because a development build rejects a patch path, the drafts are not revoked as they are when a recipe fails: they stay writable, and a second `finalize()` returns a state that can hold a revoked draft, with patches that miss changes. Create a new draft from the base state instead.

372.content: A recipe can pass a draft to a helper that calls `create()`. Unlike Immer's `produce`, which drafts the draft itself, `create()` drafts a copy of its current state, `current(draft)`: the values that the helper's recipe leaves unchanged are objects of the base state. Assigning the result back into the outer draft is safe, but changing one of those values afterwards changes the base state, because the outer draft returns an assigned value as it is (#160). Development builds warn once when `create()` receives a draft with a recipe.

373.content: To avoid it, let such a helper change a draft in place, and call `create()` only on other values:

374.content: On a draft, `rename()` returns the draft itself, so the outer recipe changes its result through the outer draft, and the values that it leaves unchanged keep their references. Unlike a call to `create()`, it changes the outer draft even if the caller discards the result.

375.content: Where that does not fit, make such changes in the helper's recipe, or through the outer draft before calling the helper. If the helper's result must not share objects with the base state, give `create()` a deep copy, as in `create(structuredClone(current(draft)), recipe)`, at the cost of copying the draft on each call and of new references for the values that the recipe leaves unchanged; `structuredClone` turns class instances into plain objects and throws on functions. To catch such writes, enable `enableAutoFreeze` in development, for example with `makeCreator({ enableAutoFreeze: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' })` for such helpers: it freezes the helper's result together with the objects of the base state that it shares, so a write to them throws instead of changing the base state, as Immer's default auto-freeze does.

376.content: A draft belongs to the `create()` call that made it, also the draft that `create(base)` returns. Do not store it in the draft of another call, or in an object that you assign there: it is revoked when its own call ends, so the other call's result can hold a draft that throws when it is read, and a Set draft that received it may no longer find it with `has()` or `delete()`. Store `current(draft)`, the original object or the result of that call instead.

377.content: The errors that `create()` throws, such as for an invalid base state or for a recipe that changes the draft and returns another value, are listed with their production codes on the errors page.

379.content: Take a snapshot of the current value of a draft, as plain objects without proxies.

382.content: `current(draft)` returns a snapshot of the current value of a draft: plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets with the changes that the recipe has made so far, without the proxies of the draft. The snapshot stays valid after the recipe ends, so it can be logged, compared, kept or searched.

383.content: The snapshot shares every object that the recipe has not changed with the base state. For a draft that the recipe has not changed, `current(draft)` returns its original value, which `original(draft)` also returns, without copying it.

384.content: A changed draft is copied, together with its changed descendants, on every call, so each call returns new objects for it. Take one snapshot for a series of reads rather than calling `current()` in a loop.

385.content: Later changes to the draft do not change the snapshot, except changes to objects that are not drafted, such as class instances that no mark makes draftable, which the snapshot shares with the draft.

386.content: `current()` does not freeze the snapshot, also with `enableAutoFreeze`.

387.content: `current()` throws for a value that is not a draft, such as the base state or a finished state; use `isDraft()` to check.

388.content: Every object read through a draft becomes a draft of its own, so `draft.list.find()` pays for a draft per visited element. Searching `current(draft.list)` reads plain values instead: the original array while the recipe has not changed it, and otherwise a copy that holds the current value of each changed element and the original object of every other one. Its indices are those of the draft, also after the recipe added, removed or moved elements. Change the match through the draft. Its elements are not drafts, so the callback must only read them.

389.content: In strict mode, development builds warn once when a recipe leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged, which is what a search through a large draft array does.

390.content: `original(draft.list)` searches the base state instead, whose indices no longer match those of the draft once the recipe has added, removed or moved elements.

394.content: Check whether a value is a draft.

396.content: `isDraft(value)` returns `true` for a draft, of the current recipe or of any other one, and `false` for any other value, including the base state, a finished state and the values that a recipe assigned.

397.content: Use it in helpers that take a draft or a plain value, for example to change a draft in place and to call `create()` for any other value, as `create()` on a draft shows. `current()` and `original()` throw for values that are not drafts.

398.content: `isDraft()` reads the value, so for a draft whose producer has ended, which Mutative revokes, it throws as any other read does.

400.content: Check whether Mutative drafts a value, optionally with a mark.

402.content: `isDraftable(value, options?)` returns `true` for a value that Mutative can draft, and which `create()` therefore accepts as its base state.

403.content: Without a mark, these values are draftable:

406.content: `Map` and `Set` instances, also of their subclasses.

407.content: Other values are not: primitives, functions, dates, class instances, objects without a prototype, and plain objects of other realms, such as iframes. A mark makes them draftable, as `markSimpleObject()` does for objects without a prototype and plain objects of other realms. Pass the same `mark` that the `create()` calls use, to get their answer:

408.content: A mark makes a value draftable when it returns `'immutable'` or a function that copies the value. A mark that returns `'mutable'` keeps a value out of drafts when a recipe reads it, but `isDraftable()` still returns `true` for plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets.

Without it, Mutative drafts only plain objects of its own realm, and `create()` throws for a base state of the other kinds.

431.content: `original(draft)` returns the value that a draft was created from: the object of the base state, without the changes that the recipe has made to it.

432.content: Use it to compare a draft with its original value, or to read the base state without creating drafts, since the original value holds no proxies.

433.content: `original()` returns the object of the base state itself, so never change it.

434.content: It throws for a value that is not a draft, such as the base state, a finished state, or a value that the recipe assigned, which Mutative does not draft. Use `isDraft()` to check.

435.content: An object of the base state is drafted when the recipe reads it, so a search of a draft array for such an object does not find it; search `original(draft.list)` for it, as in `original(draft.list).indexOf(item)`.

436.content: `original()` reflects the state before the recipe's changes, so an index found in `original(draft.list)` no longer matches the draft once the recipe has added, removed or moved elements. To search a draft array, use `current()`.

438.content: Return a value from a recipe as it is, without searching it for drafts, or return undefined.

442.content: `rawReturn(value)` wraps the value that a recipe returns, so that `create()` makes it the next state as it is, without searching it for drafts. It also makes `undefined` the next state, which a recipe that returns nothing cannot.

443.content: A recipe can return a new state instead of changing the draft. Mutative searches such a value for drafts and replaces each one with its value, so that a returned value can hold drafts, as `{ ...draft, a: 2 }` does:

444.content: That search visits every object of the returned value, which takes time for large values. `rawReturn()` skips it for a value that holds no drafts, such as a state built from scratch or an earlier state:

445.content: In the benchmark, returning a new state of 10,000 rows took 2.6 ms with the search and 0.26 µs with `rawReturn()`. Development builds warn when a returned object holds no drafts, to suggest `rawReturn()`.

446.content: Returning an earlier state is the one workload of the benchmark in which Mutative's defaults were slower than Immer's. Immer freezes each next state by default and skips frozen values when it searches a returned state for drafts, so returning a state that it had frozen earlier took it 0.79 µs at 10,000 rows, while Mutative, which does not freeze by default, searched the same state for 2.6 ms. With the same settings, Mutative was faster: 2.6 ms against 5.7 ms without auto-freeze, and 0.53 µs against 0.79 µs with it, since its production builds skip frozen values too. `rawReturn()` returns a state that holds no drafts in 0.26 µs.

447.content: Freezing by default is a trade-off rather than a shortcut. Data that is not frozen yet, such as a response parsed from JSON, has to be frozen first: returning 10,000 rows that each call creates took Immer 9.2 ms with its default, against 3.1 ms for Mutative's search and 0.23 ms with `rawReturn()`, of which creating the rows took 0.19 ms. Freezing also made Immer slower in every other workload of the selected results, such as 25.0 µs instead of 1.82 µs to update an item of 100 rows. Auto Freeze describes when freezing is worth its cost.

448.content: Never wrap a value that holds drafts. Without strict mode, Mutative does not search it, so the next state keeps those drafts, which are revoked when the recipe ends and throw when they are read. In strict mode, Mutative still searches a value that `rawReturn()` wraps and replaces its drafts, and development builds warn: `The return value contains drafts, please don't use 'rawReturn()' to wrap the return value.`

449.content: Call it with exactly one argument; it throws otherwise.

450.content: Wrap only objects and `undefined`. A recipe can return a primitive as it is, since a primitive holds no drafts, and development builds warn when `rawReturn()` receives one.

451.content: With auto-freeze, production builds do not search frozen objects in a returned value or the values they hold, so returning an earlier, frozen state, or state built from one, costs little even without `rawReturn()`. Development builds still search them and throw when they find a draft there, so never put a draft in a frozen object or in a value it holds.

452.content: Enable strict mode in development when you use `rawReturn()`, for example with `strict: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, so that a wrapped value that holds drafts is reported.

454.content: Read values that are not drafted in strict mode.

456.content: In strict mode, reading an object that Mutative does not draft throws, such as a `Date`, a class instance that no mark makes draftable, or a value that a `mark` makes mutable. `unsafe(callback)` runs the callback with such reads allowed and returns what it returns.

457.content: Strict mode makes such reads explicit because Mutative does not copy the values that it does not draft: the draft and the base state share them, so a change to one of them, such as `draft.createdAt.setFullYear(2000)`, changes the base state as well, and the next state holds the same object. Replace such values, as the recipe above replaces `updatedAt`, or mark their class as `immutable` so that Mutative drafts and copies them.

458.content: `unsafe()` allows the reads of all producers until its callback returns. A nested call keeps the access of the outer call until the outer one returns.

459.content: Outside strict mode, `unsafe()` only calls the callback.

460.content: Values that a recipe reads inside `unsafe()` are still drafts when they are draftable, so changes to them are recorded as usual.

462.content: Every difference between Mutative and Immer 11.1.18 in APIs, defaults, drafts and patches, and the behaviors that both share.

470.content: Mutative and Immer work the same way: a recipe changes a draft, and the library produces the next state, which shares every part that the recipe left unchanged. Most code moves from Immer by renaming its functions, as the migration guide shows. This page lists the differences that change what code does or produces, checked against Immer 11.1.18, and the behaviors that both libraries share where it is easy to assume otherwise.

476.content: Options per call, without global settings or plugins

479.content: Drafts of class instances without changing the class

491.content: Map and Set subclasses keep their class

494.content: ES2025 Set methods on Set drafts

497.content: Freezing reaches the objects used as Map keys

500.content: Array methods that run natively on drafts

503.content: JSON Pointer string paths in patches

512.content: `produceWithPatches()`, or a patch listener passed to `produce()`

513.content: `create(base, recipe, { enablePatches: true })`, which returns `[state, patches, inversePatches]`

519.content: The same functions; `isDraftable()` also takes `{ mark }`

531.content: `makeCreator(options)`, which returns a `create()` with these options

535.content: Not needed; array methods run natively

540.content: **Auto-freeze.** Mutative leaves results unfrozen unless `enableAutoFreeze` is set, while Immer freezes them by default. With freezing on, both freeze the whole result deeply, unchanged parts included, and freeze Map and Set instances so that their mutators throw. Mutative also freezes the objects that a Map uses as keys, which Immer leaves unfrozen.

541.content: **Options per call.** Each `create()` and `apply()` call takes its own options, and `makeCreator()` sets defaults, where Immer's `setAutoFreeze()` and its plugins change the module for every caller. Maps, Sets and patches work without the `enableMapSet()` and `enablePatches()` calls that Immer requires and throws without.

542.content: **Marking.** A `mark` function decides how values are drafted: it can make class instances draftable without changing their class, where Immer requires an `[immerable]` property on it, keep values mutable so that the recipe changes them in place, or return a function that copies a value. Mutative copies a class instance that a mark makes draftable with all its own properties, non-enumerable ones included, as Immer does with `setUseStrictShallowCopy('class_only')`, but assigns those that are enumerable, writable and configurable, as Immer's default copy does, so an own property that shadows a setter of the class runs it; see Copying marked instances. Both copy only the enumerable properties of plain objects and read their getters as values. See mark.

543.content: **Strict mode.** With `strict: true`, reading a value that the recipe could change without a draft, such as a class instance that is not marked, throws unless the read happens inside `unsafe()`. Immer has no such mode. See strict mode.

544.content: **Map and Set subclasses** keep their class and its methods, in drafts and in the next state. Immer's next state holds plain Maps and Sets instead.

545.content: **ES2025 Set methods**, such as `union()` and `isSubsetOf()`, work on Set drafts and compare objects as iterating the draft returns them; see the FAQ. On Immer's Set drafts they do not see the draft's items: `union()` of a draft of `new Set([1, 2])` with `new Set([3])` returns `Set {3}`.

546.content: **Async recipes** make `create()` return a Promise of the result, and the draft stays usable until the Promise settles; see create(). Immer 11 throws, because the returned Promise counts as a new value while the recipe changed the draft.

547.content: **A draft passed to a nested `create()`** is copied, where Immer's `produce()` drafts the draft itself; see create() on a draft.

548.content: **Returned values.** Both replace the state with a value that the recipe returns, and both throw when the recipe also changed the draft. `rawReturn()` returns `undefined`, as Immer's `nothing` does, and also returns a value without searching it for drafts; see rawReturn().

549.content: **Array methods.** `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()` and `reverse()` move the elements of a plain array on its copy, and `indexOf()`, `lastIndexOf()` and `includes()` search it natively, under the contract that the FAQ describes. Immer runs them through the proxy unless its opt-in `enableArrayMethods()` plugin is enabled, which in Immer 11.1.18 can return raw base objects and emit patches that fail to replay; see the audit.

550.content: **Alike in both.** Each path to a shared object gets its own draft; see shared references. A class instance that is neither marked nor `[immerable]` is not drafted, so a recipe that changes it changes the base state. `current()` and `original()` throw for values that are not drafts. An iteration over a Map draft that starts before the recipe changes the Map walks the base Map, in both libraries; see the FAQ.

551.content: Both libraries emit the same patches for most changes: the same operations, paths and values, the patches of nested drafts before those of their parents, and values that are the objects of the next state, frozen with it when freezing is on. They differ in the following cases; Patches describes how Mutative generates and applies them.

552.content: **Arrays that get shorter.** By default, Mutative records a shorter array with a `replace` patch of its `length`, as in the patches of `pop()` and `list.length = 0` and in the inverse patches of `push()` and of a `splice()` that inserts, while Immer removes each index with a `remove` patch. With `enablePatches: { arrayLengthAssignment: false }`, Mutative emits the same `remove` patches as Immer.

553.content: **Changed items of a Set.** When a recipe changes objects in a Set without adding or removing items, Mutative emits a `replace` patch under the position of each changed item, while Immer removes the old object and adds the new one. Once the recipe adds or removes items, both carry the changed items by value.

554.content: **String paths.** With `enablePatches: { pathAsArray: false }`, Mutative emits paths as JSON Pointer strings, as JSON Patch requires, while Immer's paths are always arrays. A string path cannot name a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key.

555.content: **Applying patches.** `apply()` takes the `enableAutoFreeze`, `strict` and `mark` options, or `mutable: true` to change the state in place and return `undefined`.

556.content: **Alike in both.** `apply()` and `applyPatches()` change a draft in place, copy patch values before applying them, accept `-` as the index that appends to an array, and reject `move`, `copy` and `test` operations and paths through `__proto__` or `constructor`. As they copy patch values, an object that patches add to a Set is a copy, which the inverse patches cannot remove, so an undo after a redo leaves it in the Set in both libraries, and both append the elements that patches add, so such a Set can hold its elements in another order; see Sets of objects.

557.content: Mutative passes the test suite of Immer, adapted to its API. The non-support tests pin cases that Immer 11.1.18 gets wrong and Mutative does not, such as a draft that escapes into the next state and Map keys that stay mutable after freezing. The array methods audit reproduces patch ordering, base mutation and draft finalization failures of Immer's `enableArrayMethods()` plugin, with reproduction tests that include plugin-disabled controls and run the same recipes against Mutative.

558.content: With matched settings, both freezing or both not and both generating patches or both not, Mutative was faster than Immer 11.1.18 in 595 of 614 measured cases, 3.6x on geometric mean. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases, 6.6x on geometric mean. Immer was faster only with auto-freeze: when updating class instances with many fields, and in two 100-row array updates whose runs overlapped those of Mutative.

559.content: With patches on and auto-freeze off, Mutative was faster in 148 of 150 cases and never slower, and faster in every array case: 4.4x Immer and 13x Mutative 1.3.0 on geometric mean. The comparisons run Immer without its `enableArrayMethods()` plugin. In Immer 11.1.18 the plugin returns raw base objects from `shift`, `pop` and `splice`, so editing them changes the previous state, and its patches can fail to replay; the audit above reproduces these failures.

560.content: Immer 11.0.0 ported the finalization callbacks of Mutative, which replace a recursive traversal of the draft tree, in immerjs/immer#1183. Immer 11.1.18, which these measurements use, includes them.
